correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s exact question. It correctly identifies the hypothesis x = \aleph_1, the relevant negative polarized partition relation on the pair (x, \omega), the intended expansion in terms of a 2-coloring with no monochromatic rectangle of sizes x and \omega, and the conclusion being asked for: whether this forces x to be the continuum \mathfrak{c}.
missing_details: The paper’s official wording is 'nicely defined invariant'; from the surrounding discussion this is meant in the setting of cardinal invariants of the continuum.
To be fully stand-alone, the partition notation should be written explicitly as \binom{x}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{x}{\omega}^{1,1}_2.

The failure of the strong polarized relation should be stated as the existence of a coloring c : x \times \omega \to 2 such that there do not exist A \subseteq x and B \subseteq \omega with |A| = x, |B| = \omega, and c constant on A \times B.
The problem is motivated by the immediately preceding rephrasing of Theorem 2.1: \mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1 implies \binom{\mathfrak{c}}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{\mathfrak{c}}{\omega}^{1,1}_2.

The nearby context explains that if x = \aleph_1 < \mathfrak{s} is consistent (for example x = \mathfrak{a} or x = \mathfrak{b}), then the positive relation can be consistent; so the real interest is in invariants at or above the splitting number. This is contextual motivation, not part of the formal statement.
refined_question: Let x be a nicely defined cardinal invariant of the continuum. Assume that whenever x = \aleph_1, the negative strong polarized relation \binom{x}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{x}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 holds; equivalently, whenever x = \aleph_1 there is a coloring c : x \times \omega \to 2 such that no sets A \subseteq x and B \subseteq \omega with |A| = x and |B| = \omega make c constant on A \times B. Must it follow that x = \mathfrak{c}?
justification: The draft is essentially a restatement of Problem 3.1. In Section 3 the authors first rephrase Theorem 2.1 as the implication \mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1 \Rightarrow \binom{\mathfrak{c}}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{\mathfrak{c}}{\omega}^{1,1}_2, and then ask whether \mathfrak{c} is the correct invariant for this negative implication. Definition 1.1 supplies the exact meaning of the strong polarized relation, so expanding the negative arrow into a coloring-with-no-monochromatic-rectangle formulation is faithful to the paper. The sentence immediately after Problem 3.1 explains the intended scope: the problem is interesting because some invariants x can consistently satisfy x = \aleph_1 while still allowing the positive relation when x < \mathfrak{s}; hence the issue is really about invariants not covered by that phenomenon. So the nearest official target is Problem 3.1, not a broader neighboring problem.
